Never. The premise is a myth: glass is an amorphous solid, not a slow-flowing liquid, and at room temperature its viscosity is so high that sagging would take far longer than the age of the universe.

Old windows are uneven because of how they were made. Crown glass was spun into discs, producing panes of varying thickness, and glaziers often installed the thicker edge down for stability. Cylinder glass had similar irregularities. Evidence against flow: medieval panes are sometimes found thicker at the top or sides, and much older glass, like Roman-era pieces and optical instruments from centuries ago, shows no sign of sagging.

Your modern float-glass windows are uniformly flat and will stay that way.
